title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: what a song can and must say

questions.prompt: Complete this exchange at the check-in desk. Tina: "The gate closes in twenty minutes — we ___ hurry." Alex: "And where ___ we get something to eat before we board?"

options.text: can … must
mustn't … can
must … can
must … must

questions.explanation: A gate that closes in twenty minutes creates a necessity, and necessity is must: we must hurry. The second blank asks where eating is possible inside the airport, and possibility is can: where can we get something to eat? Opening with can turns an emergency into a mere option; "mustn't hurry" forbids exactly what the gate demands; and "where must we get something to eat" would make eating an obligation with only one legal place for it, which no airport imposes.

questions.prompt: You have to prove that a singer felt determination during her hardest years, not just sadness. Which sentence from her interview proves it?

options.text: Those were the hardest years of my life.
I never once thought of stopping.
Other singers had all the luck.
I was afraid the phone would never ring.

questions.explanation: Determination is the refusal to give up, and only one sentence shows a refusal: she never once thought of stopping. Calling those years the hardest of her life shows sadness, which is precisely the feeling you were asked to go beyond; envying the luck of other singers shows jealousy; and a phone that never rings shows fear. Naming a feeling is half the work — the other half is pointing at the words that carry it.

questions.prompt: In a song, a woman sings that her hope is a candle no wind can blow out. Which sentence says the same thing without the image?

options.text: She lights a candle whenever she hopes.
Her hope is as small as a candle flame.
She is afraid the wind will put her candle out.
Nothing at all will ever destroy her hope.

questions.explanation: A metaphor puts one thing in the place of another: here the candle stands for the hope, and the wind for everything that could put it out. Say it without the image and you get: nothing at all will ever destroy her hope. Reading the picture literally produces a woman with a real candle, which the song never mentions; and the image insists that the flame resists — it says nothing about the hope being small, and nothing about the woman being frightened. Paraphrasing a metaphor means replacing the picture by its meaning and keeping none of the picture.

questions.prompt: A notice at the door of a recording studio reads: "You must switch your mobile phone off before you go in." Which notice forbids exactly the same thing?

options.text: You mustn't go into the studio with your phone on.
You mustn't switch your phone off before you go in.
You can't switch your phone off before you go in.
You mustn't take your phone into the studio.

questions.explanation: Turning an obligation into a prohibition means forbidding the OPPOSITE action, not the action itself: if you must switch the phone off, then what is banned is going in with it on. The two notices that forbid switching the phone off say the reverse of it, and it changes nothing that one writes mustn't and the other can't: both of them forbid, and what they forbid is the very action the notice orders. The last one goes further than the notice instead: a phone switched off but still in your pocket breaks no rule, because what is banned is the phone being on, not the phone being there.

questions.prompt: A listener has phoned a radio show to ask for a song. Put the five turns back in the order of the conversation.

options.text: Listener: The lyrics, above all. They say something I could never say myself.
Presenter: Good evening, you're on the air. Which song would you like us to play?
Presenter: Here it comes — and thank you for calling.
Presenter: A lovely choice. What do you like most in it, the melody or the lyrics?
Listener: Immortality, please. I'm crazy about it — my mother used to sing it to me.

questions.explanation: Every turn hooks on to the one before it. The presenter opens the call and asks for a title; only a title can answer that, and the listener gives one along with the reason why she loves it. "A lovely choice" comments on the title just given and narrows the question down to the melody or the lyrics; "The lyrics, above all" answers that choice and can follow nothing else; and the presenter closes by playing the song and thanking the caller. Ordering a dialogue means finding the word each turn borrows from the turn before it.

questions.prompt: To pay for Celine Dion's first record, her manager mortgaged his own house. What did he actually do?

options.text: He sold the house and moved into a flat.
He rented the house out while the record was made.
He borrowed money against the house.
He bought a second house with the record money.

questions.explanation: To mortgage a house is to give a bank the right to own it for a time in exchange for a loan: the money comes in at once, and the house stays yours as long as you keep repaying. Selling is a different act — the house is gone, and so is any way back — while renting it out or buying another one brings in nothing like the sum a first recording costs. The word measures how far the man was ready to go: he put the roof over his head at risk on one unknown twelve-year-old voice.
